jurisdiction: All of Collin County (Collin College's taxing district)
official_title: This is a tax increase. "the issuance of $600,000,000 in bonds for college facilities used for workforce training, career and technical education, and academic instruction, and the levy of taxes sufficient to pay the principal and interest on the bonds."
plain_summary: Lets Collin College borrow up to $600 million for buildings used for workforce training, career and technical education and academic classes, and levy a property tax to repay it. The college says it would expand eight campuses and build new campuses in Anna and Royse City and an aviation academy in McKinney. In Allen, campus renovations would add classroom and lab space and room for automotive and diesel technology programs (Community Impact).
yes_means: A YES vote lets Collin College sell up to $600 million in bonds for new and expanded campus buildings, repaid with property taxes.
no_means: A NO vote means the college can't sell these bonds. College President Neil Matkin said it would then “figure out alternative financing or we’d slow the projects down until we could figure out a way to afford them” (Community Impact).
current_law: Collin County voters approved a $600 million Collin College bond in 2017 (college FAQ). This bond would pay for phases 2 and 3 of the college's Destination 2030 plan; enrollment grew 11.92% from 2017 to 2024 and its campuses average about 20 years old (Community Impact). Without it the college can't sell these bonds.
fiscal_impact: Principal $600,000,000; estimated interest $378,192,750; total $978,192,750 over 20 years (the voter information document in the college's notice of election). The document puts the largest yearly increase on a $100,000 homestead at $20.18 and says "this figure makes conservative assumptions"; it assumes taxable values grow 4% for one year and then stay flat. The college already owes $438,250,000 in principal and $132,004,735 in interest. Its tax rate has been $0.08122 per $100 since 2018, and the college says it is "anticipated to stay at the same rate with the passage of the 2026 bond" (college financial impact page).

It starts with "This is a tax increase" (printed in capitals) because state law requires that wording on bonds repaid by property taxes even if the rate stays the same, Equity Center director Josh Sanderson told Community Impact; Matkin said the college's rate is expected to stay the same. A tax bill can still change with property values: the Murphy Monitor notes "an individual’s total property tax bill could still change if appraised property values increase." An Allen ballot has two "Prop A" items that are separate votes: this one and Collin County's Prop A (courts and jail). In a small part of far northern Allen there is also McKinney ISD's Prop A.

supporters_case.text: No organized campaign for or against the college bond was found as of Oct. 29, 2026. Matkin: “We’re going to continue to sell bonds when the financial circumstances surrounding it allow us to keep our word and do the right thing.” Frisco Chamber of Commerce President Christal Howard: “Workforce availability is one of the biggest factors that affects a business’s ability to succeed and grow” (Community Impact). jurisdiction: McKinney ISD (most of McKinney, plus a small, mostly commercial part of far northern Allen near US 75 and SH 121)
official_title: This is a tax increase. "Ratifying the ad valorem tax rate of $1.0664 per $100 valuation in the McKinney Independent School District for the current year, a rate that will result in an increase of 4.4222 percent in maintenance and operations tax revenue for the District for the current year as compared to the preceding year, which is an additional $9,142,763."
plain_summary: Asks you to approve McKinney ISD's school tax rate of $1.0664 per $100 of value for this year. Its operating part, $0.7464, is about 3.17 cents above the most the district can set without a vote. The district says the extra money, $9.1 million a year before the state takes some back through recapture and about $4.1 million after, would go to teacher pay and student programs (Community Impact). Even with Prop A, the total rate is 3.79 cents lower than last year's $1.1043, because the state lowered the operating rate and the district lowered its debt rate (district financial page).
yes_means: A YES vote approves the $1.0664 rate, including about 3.17 cents per $100 above the state limit for the district's operating budget.
no_means: A NO vote sets the rate at the most allowed without a vote, about $1.0347 per $100 (the district's $0.7147 operating rate plus its $0.32 debt rate), and the district doesn't get the extra operating money. The district says it "would face reductions that could affect student programming, campus staffing, transportation services and the overall classroom experience" (district Prop A page).
current_law: Texas caps the tax rate a school district can set for day-to-day costs; going above it takes voter approval (Texas Tax Code 26.08). McKinney ISD adopted its 2026-27 budget with a projected $6 million shortfall, its third year in a row, after closing Eddins, McNeil and Wolford elementaries at the end of 2025-26 to save about $3 million a year (Community Impact).
fiscal_impact: Per the district's notice of the tax rate election: the $1.0664 rate ($0.7464 operating, $0.3200 debt) brings in $9,142,763 more operating revenue than last year, about 4.4222% more. The district's chief financial officer, Marlene Harbeson, said recapture (money Texas takes back from districts with high property wealth) leaves about $4.1 million of it (Community Impact). The district's financial page puts the median homestead bill at $3,925, down from $4,227, as the median value falls from $382,757 to $368,036; those figures multiply the rate by the full value, before the homestead exemption.
confusing_wording_note: A “VATRE” is a voter-approval tax rate election: the vote Texas requires when a school district wants an operating tax rate above the state's cap. The ballot says "This is a tax increase" (printed in capitals) because the rate is above that cap and operating revenue goes up, even though the district's total rate is lower than last year's. The ballot doesn't say the extra is about 3.17 cents or that the total rate fell. The district's Prop A web page prints the rate as $1.0644; the ballot and the official notice say $1.0664. McKinney ISD covers most of McKinney and only a small, mostly commercial part of far northern Allen near US 75 and SH 121; most Allen homes are in Allen ISD, which has nothing on this ballot. An Allen ballot can have three separate "Prop A" items: Collin County's (courts and jail), Collin College's (campuses) and this one.

supporters_case.text: A political committee, Vote For McKinney ISD, reported raising $43,500 and spending $281 from July 1 to Sept. 24, 2026 (its report filed Oct. 4). The district: "Prop A is not a building bond. It funds the people in the classroom." Trustee Corey Homer: “We’ve done everything that we can do except go before the voters” (Community Impact). Board President Amy Dankel: “It's important for voters to know that, although the wording of these bond proposals (set by the state) sounds a little wonky, their taxes will actually be going down” (Community Impact).

opponents_case.text: We could not confirm an organized campaign against McKinney ISD's propositions as of Oct. 29, 2026. McKinney ISD parent Anthony England: “I would love to vote yes ... I think it's hard seeing the lack of transparency in the school closure process, especially knowing that the VATRE was an option that wasn't offered to my kids to keep their schools open” (Community Impact).

explainers.title: Bond on the ballot: McKinney ISD officials call $500M bond, tax rate election this November

jurisdiction: McKinney ISD (most of McKinney, plus a small, mostly commercial part of far northern Allen near US 75 and SH 121)
short_title: McKinney stadium turf and track bonds
official_title: This is a property tax increase. "The issuance of $2,550,000 of bonds by the McKinney Independent School District for designing, renovating, improving, upgrading, updating, acquiring, and equipping existing stadium facilities and related infrastructure and the levying of a tax sufficient to pay the principal of and interest on the bonds."
plain_summary: Lets McKinney ISD borrow up to $2.55 million to replace turf and track at its existing stadiums, and levy a property tax to repay it (Community Impact).
yes_means: A YES vote lets the district sell up to $2.55 million in bonds for stadium turf and track, repaid with property taxes.
no_means: A NO vote means the district can't sell these bonds.
current_law: Without Prop E the district can't sell these bonds.
fiscal_impact: Principal $2,550,000; estimated interest $1,227,709; total $3,777,709 over 20 years at no more than 5% interest (the voter information document in the district's notice of bond election). Estimated largest yearly tax increase for this proposition on a homestead with $100,000 of taxable value after the $140,000 homestead exemption: $0, with what the document calls "conservative assumptions" about value growth. The district already owes $338,220,000 in principal and $89,536,726 in interest on earlier bonds.
confusing_wording_note: The ballot says "This is a property tax increase" (printed in capitals), wording state law requires on school bonds repaid by property taxes even if the rate stays the same; the district estimates $0 more a year for these bonds, and its debt rate fell from $0.37 to $0.32 this year. McKinney ISD's Props B to E are separate from Collin County's Props B to D on the same ballot. McKinney ISD covers most of McKinney and only a small, mostly commercial part of far northern Allen near US 75 and SH 121; most Allen homes are in Allen ISD, which has nothing on this ballot.

supporters_case.text: A political committee, Vote For McKinney ISD, reported raising $43,500 and spending $281 from July 1 to Sept. 24, 2026 (its report filed Oct. 4). Chief Financial Officer Marlene Harbeson: “Together, the bond and VATRE help ensure the district can accommodate growth, maintain and improve facilities, invest in students and staff and preserve financial stability without diverting operating funds away from educational programs” (Community Impact).
